subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of a low-pressure invitation [Thinking]
passage: On the walk home along the canal, Keerthana practised under her breath. Tomorrow the quiz club was meeting at the town library to prepare for the district round, and she wanted to ask Ravi from the next section to join. Not a date. Just the group. She tried it: "We're practising for the quiz at the library tomorrow, four o'clock. You're good at geography, if you want to come." Then she added, "It's fine if you're busy." That part mattered. She pictured Ravi saying no. Okay, then: "No problem, see you around." And a smile. She pictured him saying yes. "Great, it's upstairs." Dolma, walking beside her, asked what she was mumbling. "Nothing," said Keerthana, and then, "Okay, fine. Listen to this and tell me it's not weird."

qa.q: When and where was the quiz club meeting?
qa.a: At the town library, at four o'clock tomorrow.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana picture both a yes and a no?
qa.a: She wanted to feel calm and prepared, so a no wouldn't sting or make things awkward.

qa.q: What makes "It's fine if you're busy" important?
qa.a: It makes the invitation easy to decline, so Ravi won't feel pushed into saying yes.

qa.q: How might Dolma react to Keerthana's rehearsal?
qa.a: Dolma, curious about the mumbling, may be amused and supportive once Keerthana shares the lines.

grounding: Shows a student mentally rehearsing an easy-to-decline invitation to a group study session and preparing calm replies to either answer.
